definition: DATR is a language for lexical knowledge representation.
details: The lexical knowledge is encoded in a network of nodes. Each node has a set of attributes encoded with it. A node can represent a word or a word form. DATR was developed in the late 1980s by Roger Evans, Gerald Gazdar and Bill Keller, and used extensively in the 1990s; the standard specification is contained in the Evans and Gazdar RFC, available on the Sussex website (below). DATR has been implemented in a variety of programming languages, and several implementations are available on the internet, including an RFC compliant implementation at the Bielefeld website (below). DATR is still used for encoding inheritance networks in various linguistic and non-linguistic domains and is under discussion as a standard notation for the representation of lexical information.

explainer.lead: DATR is a language for organising lexical knowledge as a network of nodes, with attributes attached to each node. It allows information about words and word forms to be shared through inheritance, and the same approach can also encode non-linguistic knowledge.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a set of connected index cards, where each card describes a word or one of its forms and lists important facts about it. Connections let cards share information instead of copying the same facts onto every card. DATR is a language for writing down this kind of network.
tiers.practitioner: A DATR description represents words or word forms as nodes and encodes their attributes within an inheritance network. Implementations exist in several programming languages, including an RFC-compliant implementation at Bielefeld; the Evans and Gazdar RFC is the standard specification. When working across implementations, the RFC provides the common reference point.
tiers.paperLevel: A DATR description is a network N of nodes, where each node n has an associated set of encoded attributes A(n); a node may denote a word or a word form. The language encodes inheritance networks for lexical information and can also be applied outside linguistics. DATR was developed in the late 1980s by Roger Evans, Gerald Gazdar and Bill Keller, and its standard specification is the Evans and Gazdar RFC.

explainer.example: Consider a network describing the verb walk and its word form walked. General attributes associated with walk can be represented at its node, while the walked node carries information specific to that form, allowing shared lexical knowledge to remain connected rather than duplicated in two isolated entries.

usedIn.name: Lexical knowledge representation
usedIn.detail: Encoding words, word forms and their associated attributes.

usedIn.name: Linguistic inheritance networks
usedIn.detail: Organising linguistic information so that nodes can share inherited knowledge.

usedIn.name: Non-linguistic knowledge representation
usedIn.detail: Applying the same inheritance-network notation beyond lexical domains.

explainer.intuition: DATR treats lexical knowledge as connected descriptions rather than a pile of independent entries. Nodes hold attributes, while the network and its inheritance structure let related descriptions share information.
howItWorks: Create nodes for the words or word forms being described.
Attach the relevant attributes to each node.
Connect the nodes in a network that encodes inheritance.
Use the resulting network to represent shared and specific lexical information.
explainer.whyItMatters: DATR provides a compact way to organise lexical information and express relationships between descriptions. Its continued use for inheritance networks and its discussion as a standard notation reflect its role beyond a single implementation or research project.
misconceptions: DATR is a representation language, not one particular software implementation.
It describes networks of related information, not just isolated dictionary entries.
Its inheritance networks can represent non-linguistic knowledge as well as lexical knowledge.
